This is a rider-filed dangerous-driving allegation (speeding, hard braking, shoulder overtaking) on a completed RydeX trip Jurong East MRT → NUS, 21:22–21:34 [F1][F2]. Because the case involves an allegation of dangerous driving, the correct disposition is escalation for human handling rather than auto-adjudication [SAFE-2]. Both advocates converge on this outcome (C1, C2, D1, D5, D4 revised ask), so no monetary ruling is made [SAFE-2].

The threat-keyword limb of the safety rule is not engaged: the only chat messages are ordinary pickup logistics — the rider at the main entrance in a blue shirt at 21:18 [F3] and the driver stating arrival in 2 min in a white Honda Vezel at 21:19 [F4]; the driver's statement is a denial, not a threat [F5][SAFE-1]. The escalation therefore rests solely on the dangerous-driving limb [SAFE-2], not on any abuse or intimidation language [F3][F4][F5][SAFE-1].

What happened, per the record: the trip covered 8.5 km against an 8.6 km optimal route (−0.1 km) [F1], completed in 12.8 min against a 14 min estimate (−1.0 min) [F2]. The dispute: whether the driver drove in an unsafe manner during that run. The GPS facts give only distance and duration — there is no speed, acceleration, braking or lane-position telemetry in the table [F1][F2][F5]. The rider's account of shoulder overtaking and hard braking is therefore supported only by her own statement [F5], and no fact in the table either confirms or disproves it [F1][F2][SAFE-2]. The 1.0 min under-run is equally consistent with light traffic at 21:22 or a favourable light cycle and is not a speed measurement [F2][SAFE-2].

For the human reviewer to check: (i) any available telematics / harsh-driving or speed exceptions for the 21:22–21:34 window on the NUS corridor [F1][F2]; (ii) the driver's statement that the rider was on the phone and raised no complaint in-trip [F5], noting a user-submitted statement cannot by itself resolve the allegation; (iii) whether the clean 90-day records on both sides — rider 0 disputes / 0 upheld over 1308 days [F6], driver 0 disputes / 0 upheld over 345 trips in 90 days, rating 4.82 [F7] — bear on credibility; profiles do not decide the case either way [F6][F7][SAFE-2].

No fare issue arises: the RydeX fare is a fixed quote of $21.04 and the actual distance (8.5 km) is not longer than the optimal route (8.6 km) [F1], so there is no excess-distance or unpublished-surcharge head to refund [FARE-1][RD-2]; and RD-2 has no application absent an off-route segment [F1][RD-1]. No SAFE-1 or NS-1/RD-6 account-action condition is met on these facts [F3][F4][F5][F7][SAFE-1][RD-6].

claims.assertion: This ticket is a dangerous-driving safety allegation by the rider (speeding, hard braking, shoulder overtaking), so it must be routed to human review rather than auto-adjudicated, with a fact summary attached.

No in-app chat message or driver statement contains any threat, intimidation, harassment or abuse language (F3 and F4 are ordinary pickup coordination; F5 is a denial), so the threat-keyword escalation path is not the one that applies here; the escalation rests on the dangerous-driving limb of the safety rule.

The GPS record is consistent with a hurried, non-stop run rather than a normal-paced trip: the driver covered the optimal-route distance in 12.8 min against a 14 min estimate (F2) with no deviation (F1), i.e. no detour or stop that would absorb the last 1.0 min — it supports the rider's account of continuously pushing the pace, though it is not a speed measurement.

The fare cannot be challenged as an overcharge: the trip is a fixed-quote RydeX fare of $21.04 and the distance actually driven (8.5 km, F1) is not longer than the optimal route (8.6 km, F1), so there is no route-deviation refund head to claim.

The rider's complaint is not a bare assertion contradicted by system records: she has 0 prior disputes and 0 upheld in 90 days on a 3.6-year-old account (F6), and the driver had never been the subject of a dispute before (F7), so neither side's 90-day record supplies a reason to discount the report; the account records support a review request, not a finding of fault.

weaknesses: There is no GPS speed, acceleration, braking or lane-position telemetry in the fact table — F1 and F2 give only distance and duration, so the shoulder-overtaking and hard-braking allegations are supported by nothing but the rider's own statement, and the system records do not confirm them.

F2 (12.8 min actual vs 14 min estimate) is a single-fact 1.0 min difference and is equally consistent with light traffic or a favourable light cycle — the judge is entitled to read it as neutral rather than as evidence of speeding.

The driver's statement F5 denies any complaint being raised during the trip and says the rider was on her phone throughout; the chat (F3, F4) is silent on driving, so no contemporaneous in-app protest exists to corroborate the rider's account.

The driver's profile F7 (4.82 rating, 345 trips in 90 d, 0 disputes/0 upheld) is a strong counterweight a judge may weigh against a one-off safety report, and no clause lets a clean history be used to establish the safety event either way.

The requested remedy is procedural only: SAFE-2 produces no refund, and there is no fare clause hook — F1 shows no excess distance on a fixed-quote RydeX fare, so the only money the rider could recover is $0 on the merits.

claims.assertion: The GPS record shows the driver took the shortest route, not a deviating one: actual distance 8.5 km is marginally under the 8.6 km optimal route (-0.1 km, -1%), so there is no off-route or detour segment and no unsafe overtaking manoeuvre evidenced by the track.

The trip was completed faster than estimated (12.8 min actual vs 14 min estimated, -1.0 min) over an 8.6 km Jurong East MRT to NUS run, which is consistent with normal pace and not with the sustained speeding alleged in the complaint.

On the fare side the rider was charged a fixed RydeX price of $21.04 for a completed trip with no excess distance billed, so no refund is computable and no billing clause provides a ground for a refund in this case.

The driver's record shows 1263 days on the platform, a 4.82 rating over 345 trips in 90 days and zero disputes or upheld complaints in 90 days, which is inconsistent with a pattern of dangerous driving.

The rider rated 4.5 with 0 disputes in 90 days raised no in-trip safety complaint to the driver; the only record of a problem is the post-trip report, and the driver's statement is that the rider was on the phone throughout and never complained.

There is no threat, harassment, assault or dangerous-driving evidence in the in-app messages, which contain only neutral pickup logistics (rider at main entrance at 21:18, driver arriving in 2 min at 21:19 in a white Honda Vezel), so no chat-based safety clause is engaged.

weaknesses: The complaint is a first-hand safety allegation and there is no system record that can affirmatively disprove speeding or hard braking: the GPS facts (F1, F2) give only distance and duration, so they do not rule out harsh driving within the normal speed limit. The rider will rely on F1/F2 being silent on driving behaviour.

The trip was completed 1.0 min faster than estimated (F2), which the rider can argue supports the speeding allegation; the driver has no telematics record (no harsh-braking or speeding fact exists) to rebut it.
The driver's statement in F5 that the rider never complained is user-submitted and, under the system-records-priority rule, cannot by itself defeat the rider's account; it is corroborative only.
The rider has a clean record (F6), so no credibility discount can be drawn against the complainant, and profile facts cannot decide the case in the driver's favour in any event.

points.response: Conceded on the routing point: F1 (8.5 km actual vs 8.6 km optimal, -0.1 km) shows no detour, but I never claimed one — my case is the manner of driving, which the distance track cannot speak to, so D1 answers an allegation the rider did not make.

F2 cuts both ways and the driver's own reading is the weaker one: a 12.8 min run over the 8.6 km optimal route is 1.0 min faster than the 14 min estimate, and F1 shows no stop or detour that could have absorbed that minute, so the record is consistent with a driver pushing the pace rather than with a relaxed trip; it is an indicator of pace, not proof of lawful driving.
Accepted, and irrelevant: I seek no refund, so the absence of an excess-distance charge (F1) leaves the escalation request in my C1 wholly untouched.

A clean history is a mitigating profile, not evidence about this 12.8 min trip, and the driver's 0 upheld disputes (F7) is identical to the rider's 0 upheld disputes (F6), so neither profile breaks the tie; RD-6 governs repeated route violations and can never be used to establish or defeat a SAFE-2 dangerous-driving escalation.

The fact the driver relies on is his own written statement (F5), which as user-submitted content loses to system records and cannot rebut the rider's first-hand account, and the chat (F3, F4) is silent on driving — silence on safety is not evidence of safety; the absence of an in-trip protest is explained by the rider not wanting to confront the driver mid-journey.

Correct that SAFE-1 is not engaged — I conceded as much in my C2 — but the escalation rests on SAFE-2, which needs only an allegation of dangerous driving, not a keyword in the chat (F3, F4), so D6 does not remove the escalation ground.

The escalation stands unchanged: the rider's allegations of speeding, hard braking and shoulder overtaking are first-hand and the fact table contains no telematics or traffic record contradicting them, so SAFE-2 requires human review with a written fact summary (ride B-0046, Jurong East MRT to NUS, 21:22 to 21:34), and the driver's request for the same outcome confirms escalate is the only action the facts can support.
points.void_reason: citation check: a rebuttal point must cite at least one fact and one clause

points.response: Conceded on routing: the driver does not oppose escalation of a dangerous-driving allegation for human review, because the fact table contains no speed, acceleration, braking or lane-position telemetry — F1 gives only distance and F2 only duration — so the driver asks that the summary record that the system records neither confirm nor disprove the rider's account.

Agreed and it helps the driver: the messages contain only ordinary pickup coordination (rider at the main entrance at 21:18, driver arriving in 2 min at 21:19) and a denial, so no threat-keyword escalation path is engaged and the case carries no SAFE-1 finding against the driver.

The 1.0 min under-run is neutral, not corroboration: F2 shows 12.8 min actual against 14 min estimated on a route F1 shows as optimal (8.5 km vs 8.6 km), so the saving is equally explained by normal driving, light traffic at 21:22, or a favourable light cycle, and neither fact is a speed measurement.

The rider's own point confirms there is no money on the table: the RydeX fare is a fixed quote and F1 shows no excess distance, so no refund head exists and nothing in this case supports a charge against the driver's earnings.

The rider is right that profiles cannot decide fault on either side, and her clean 90-day record (0 disputes, 0 upheld) does not outweigh the driver's own clean record of 345 trips and 0 upheld disputes in 90 days (F7) on a 3.5-year account; neither profile converts an unverified allegation into a finding against the driver.
The driver's route claim stands and is unchallenged: F1 shows no over-distance and no off-route segment (actual 8.5 km vs optimal 8.6 km), so no RD-1 breach and no RD-2 refund attaches to this trip.
